summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Distributed representations blend two competing strategies—composition and superposition—that trade off and should be told apart.
summaries.question: How do superposition and composition relate as forms of distributed representation? (a conceptual analysis)

summaries.title: Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition
summaries.gist: Neural codes for shapes and colors reveal two distinct kinds of distributed representation, feature composition and superposition, each with different tradeoffs.
summaries.question: How do local, compositional, and dense neural codes differ in representing shapes and colors? (three examples)

summaries.title: Local vs Distributed Codes
summaries.gist: Distributed representations may combine two separable ideas, composition and superposition, which the note illustrates using Thorpe's four example neural codes for colored shapes.

summaries.title: "Local" Codes
summaries.gist: A pure local code assigns one neuron per shape-color pair, letting any subset of stimuli be linearly selected later, though it wastes many neurons.

summaries.title: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes
summaries.gist: Encoding independent color and shape features that compose together lets networks use far fewer neurons, generalize across new combinations, and remain interpretable.

summaries.title: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes
summaries.gist: Superposition packs many more objects into fewer neurons than composition allows, but sacrifices linear probing of features and the ability to represent in-between blends.

summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition are not points on one spectrum of distributedness but competing ways to use a fixed representational capacity.
summaries.question: Why are composition and superposition competing rather than complementary strategies? (a capacity argument)

summaries.title: Distributed Codes Aren't One Spectrum
summaries.gist: Though local, semi-local, and highly-distributed codes look like points on one spectrum of distributedness, they actually reflect two orthogonal strategies, composition and superposition.

summaries.title: Allocating Exponential Volume
summaries.gist: With a fixed number of bits, a code can either compose exponentially many feature combinations or store exponentially many separate items in superposition, but not both.

summaries.title: Mixing Composition and Superposition
summaries.gist: Sparse, rarely-combined features leave gaps in representational space that networks can fill with superposed features, letting both strategies mix.
summaries.question: How can sparse composition coexist with superposition in one code? (an example, the semi-distributed code)

summaries.title: Sparse Composition Enables Superposition
summaries.gist: When feature combinations are common, only one feature fits per neuron, but when combinations are rare, the unused combinatorial space can hold extra features in superposition.

summaries.title: The Semi-Distributed Code
summaries.gist: Thorpe's semi-distributed code composes color and shape features while placing each set in mutual superposition, so features exist as neuron-direction combinations rather than single units.

summaries.title: Conclusion
summaries.gist: Distinguishing composition from superposition matters because only composition lets us understand networks through a small number of independent features.
summaries.question: Why does distinguishing composition from superposition matter for interpretability? (a summary claim)

summaries.title: Two Kinds of Distributed Representation
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition, though mixable, are fundamentally in tension, and only composition lets networks be understood via a linear number of independent features instead of exponential volume.

glossary.name: Superposition
glossary.senseHere: Packing more features into a representation than there are neurons, by giving each neuron several overlapping meanings rather than one. This only works if the features are rarely all present at once, and reading them back out needs a nonlinear step, unlike composition.

glossary.name: Distributed representation
glossary.senseHere: A representation where information about a stimulus is spread across multiple active neurons rather than one dedicated neuron per stimulus. The piece's central claim is that this umbrella phrase actually hides two different, competing strategies: composition and superposition.
glossary.background: A long-standing idea in neuroscience and connectionist AI holding that concepts are encoded across patterns of neural activity rather than by single dedicated cells.

glossary.name: Composition
glossary.senseHere: Building a representation of a whole object out of separate, independent feature-neurons that combine, such as one neuron for color and another for shape jointly encoding a colored shape. It lets a network generalize across combinations it never saw, but the exponential number of possible combinations must each get their own volume, so it competes with superposition for the same limited space.

glossary.name: Thorpe's four example codes
glossary.senseHere: Four illustrative ways neurons could encode (shape, color) pairs, ranging from one neuron per combination up to only four neurons handling everything, that the piece reinterprets not as one continuum from local to distributed but as different mixes of composition and superposition.
glossary.background: Simon Thorpe, a neuroscientist, proposed these examples in a 1989 paper to illustrate possibilities between fully local and fully distributed neural codes.

glossary.name: Linear probe
glossary.senseHere: A simple linear function trained on a network's internal activity to check whether some concept, like 'red', can be read out. The piece warns that a probe succeeding does not prove the network actually has a dedicated 'red' feature, since even a local code without any true feature for 'red' would still let a probe find it.

glossary.name: Monosemantic / polysemantic
glossary.senseHere: A monosemantic neuron responds to one single feature or meaning, as in the local code where each neuron means one exact (shape, color) pair. A polysemantic neuron responds to several unrelated features at once, which is what makes superposition and the semi-distributed code possible.
